q: In Datadog APM, what does a span represent?
options: The full record of one request across every service it touched
A logical unit of work in a distributed system for a given period
A group of related endpoints, queries, or jobs in an application
explanation: Datadog defines a span as a logical unit of work in a distributed system for a given period. Multiple spans make up a trace.
notes: That is a trace: it tracks the time spent processing a request and is made of one or more spans.
Correct: a span is one timed unit of work, for example a single DB query or an HTTP handler.
That is a service, the APM grouping of related endpoints, queries, or jobs.

q: Your `web-store` APM page lists `GET /productpage` and `ShoppingCartController#checkout`. In APM terms, what are these two entries?
options: Resources
Services
Root spans
explanation: A resource is a particular domain of an application, typically an instrumented web endpoint, database query, or background job. Datadog uses `GET /productpage` and `ShoppingCartController#checkout` as its own examples of resources.
notes: Correct: endpoints, queries, and jobs inside a service are resources.
The service is `web-store` itself, the group these endpoints belong to.
A root span is the first span of one trace (the entry point of a request), not a listed endpoint.

q: You want to trace a Python app's supported web framework and database calls without changing any code. How do you start `app.py`?
options: `DD_TRACE_ENABLED=true python app.py`
`DD_APM_ENABLED=true python app.py`
`ddtrace-run python app.py`
explanation: Prefixing the entry-point command with `ddtrace-run` auto-instruments supported web frameworks and database modules with no code changes.
notes: `DD_TRACE_ENABLED` turns tracing on or off (it defaults to `true`), but it does not load the tracer into a plain `python` run.
`DD_APM_ENABLED` is an Agent setting that controls whether the Agent accepts traces; it does nothing to the application.
Correct: `ddtrace-run <command>` loads `ddtrace` and patches supported libraries automatically.

q: The Datadog Agent is already running on the host. Which command installs the Python tracing library, which also provides the `ddtrace-run` command?
options: `pip install ddtrace`
`pip install ddtrace-run`
`pip install datadog-agent`
explanation: The Python setup docs install the tracer with `pip install ddtrace` (pip 18.0.0 or later). `ddtrace-run` is a command that comes with that package.
notes: Correct: `pip install ddtrace` installs the tracer and the `ddtrace-run` wrapper.
`ddtrace-run` is a command from the `ddtrace` package, not a separate package to install.
The Agent is a separate prerequisite installed with its own installer, not a Python package added to the app.

q: You run `ddtrace-run --info` to check your tracer setup. Which statement about its output is true?
options: It lists the traces your app sent to the Agent in the last 15 minutes
It shows a health check and configuration, but not changes made in code
It tails the Agent's trace receiver log for requests arriving on port `8126`
explanation: `ddtrace-run --info` prints a health check and the tracer configuration. It reflects environment variables only, so settings changed in application code at runtime do not appear.
notes: It reports configuration, not trace data. Search sent traces in the Trace Explorer.
Correct: use it to confirm environment-based configuration; code-level overrides are not reflected.
It reads the tracer's own configuration and does not read Agent logs.

q:
This function runs inside a request already traced by the Flask integration:
from ddtrace.trace import tracer

def checkout(cart):
    with tracer.trace("checkout.charge", resource="charge_card") as span:
        span.set_tag("cart.items", len(cart))
        charge_card(cart)
What does it produce?
options: A new trace with `checkout.charge` as root span, separate from the request's trace
A new service named `checkout.charge` in the APM service list, with `charge_card` as its only resource
A tagged `checkout.charge` child span of the request span, closed when the block exits
explanation: `tracer.trace()` activates and returns a new span that inherits from the current active span. Used as a context manager, the span finishes automatically when the block exits, and `set_tag` adds the `cart.items` tag.
notes: A new span becomes the child of the active span, so it joins the existing request trace.
The first argument is the span (operation) name. The service only changes if you pass `service=`.
Correct: it is a child span with a custom resource and tag, closed at the end of the `with` block.

q: Which `ddtrace` API traces an entire function when you apply it as a decorator?
options: `tracer.current_span()`
`@tracer.wrap()`
`tracer.configure(trace_processors=[...])`
explanation: `tracer.wrap()` is the decorator for tracing a whole function; each call creates a span.
notes: `current_span()` returns the active span so you can tag it. It does not create spans.
Correct: `@tracer.wrap()` creates a span around every call of the decorated function.
This registers trace filters (processors) that run before traces are sent. It does not trace a function.

q: A Flask app runs under `ddtrace-run`. Inside a request handler, you want the customer ID of that request as a tag on the active span. Which line do you add?
options: `tracer.current_span().set_tag("customer.id", customer_id)`
`with tracer.trace("customer.id"): ...` around the handler body
Set `DD_TAGS=customer.id:<id>` in the app's environment before it starts
explanation: `tracer.current_span()` returns the active span in the current execution context, and `set_tag` sets a key/value pair on it, so the tag lands on the span already being traced.
notes: Correct: get the active span and tag it with the per-request value.
This creates a new child span named `customer.id` instead of tagging the existing span.
`DD_TAGS` sets static global tags on every span of the process, so it cannot vary per request.

q: During an incident, you set `DD_TRACE_ENABLED=false` on one instrumented Python service and restart it. What happens?
options: The Agent on that host stops accepting traces from all applications
Only the integrations listed in `DD_PATCH_MODULES` keep sending traces
That app stops sending trace data, though instrumentation still runs
explanation: `DD_TRACE_ENABLED` (default `true`) enables or disables tracing in the SDK. When it is disabled, instrumentation still runs but no trace data is sent.
notes: That is the Agent-side `DD_APM_ENABLED` setting. `DD_TRACE_ENABLED` affects only the app that sets it.
`DD_PATCH_MODULES` chooses which modules are patched. It does not override a global tracing switch.
Correct: tracing is off for this app only. Use `DD_TRACE_<INTEGRATION>_ENABLED` to disable one integration.

q:
An application container has this environment, and the Agent runs in a container named `datadog-agent`:
DD_AGENT_HOST=datadog-agent
DD_SERVICE=checkout
DD_ENV=prod
What does the `DD_AGENT_HOST` line do?
options: It turns on the trace receiver inside the `datadog-agent` container
It points the tracer at the `datadog-agent` container (port `8126`)
It sends traces straight to Datadog, skipping the local Agent
explanation: `DD_AGENT_HOST` is read by the tracer and sets the host it submits traces to. With no `DD_TRACE_AGENT_PORT` set, it uses the default port `8126`.
notes: The tracer in the app reads this variable. The Agent's trace receiver is controlled by `DD_APM_ENABLED`, which defaults to `true`.
Correct: point `DD_AGENT_HOST` at the Agent container's name. Port `8126` is the default, so `DD_TRACE_AGENT_PORT` can be left unset.
The tracer still sends to an Agent; this setting only changes which host that Agent is on.

q: The Agent runs in its own Docker container with port `8126/tcp` published. An app in a different container has `DD_AGENT_HOST` set correctly, but no traces arrive. Which Agent setting is most likely missing?
options: `DD_APM_NON_LOCAL_TRAFFIC=true`
`DD_APM_ENABLED=true`
`DD_TRACE_ENABLED=true`
explanation: By default the Agent's trace receiver accepts only local traffic (`DD_APM_NON_LOCAL_TRAFFIC` defaults to `false`). To trace from other containers, set it to `true` on the Agent.
notes: Correct: this lets the Agent accept traces from outside its own container.
`DD_APM_ENABLED` already defaults to `true`; the Trace Agent is on by default since Agent 6.0.0.
`DD_TRACE_ENABLED` is a tracer (app-side) setting that defaults to `true`; it is not set on the Agent.

q: Which describes the default path of traces from a `ddtrace`-instrumented app to Datadog?
options: App straight to Datadog's trace intake over `8126/TCP`, with no Agent involved in the path
App to the Agent's DogStatsD port `8125/UDP`, then the Agent forwards them to Datadog over `443`
App to the local Agent on `8126/TCP`, then the Agent forwards them to Datadog over `443`
explanation: The tracer submits to the Agent's trace receiver on port `8126/TCP`. The Agent forwards APM data to the `trace.agent.<YOUR_DATADOG_SITE>` endpoint, and most Agent data goes out on port `443` over SSL.
notes: `8126` is the Agent's local receiver port, not a Datadog intake port.
`8125/UDP` is DogStatsD for custom metrics, not traces.
Correct: the tracer sends to the Agent on 8126, and the Agent forwards over HTTPS/443.

q:
A service starts with:
DD_AGENT_HOST=10.0.0.5
DD_TRACE_AGENT_URL=unix:///var/run/datadog/apm.socket
Where does the tracer send traces?
options: To `10.0.0.5:8126`, because `DD_AGENT_HOST` is more specific
To the Unix domain socket, because `DD_TRACE_AGENT_URL` takes priority
To both, so a copy reaches each Agent endpoint
explanation: `DD_TRACE_AGENT_URL` takes priority over the Agent host and port settings, and `DD_AGENT_HOST` is ignored when it is set. The URL can be `http://` or `unix://`.
notes: `DD_AGENT_HOST` is ignored whenever `DD_TRACE_AGENT_URL` is set.
Correct: the URL wins. Without either setting, the default is the UDS `/var/run/datadog/apm.socket` if it exists, otherwise `http://localhost:8126`.
The tracer submits to a single endpoint and does not duplicate traces.

q: Which three environment variables let the Python tracer apply the unified service tags?
options: `DD_SERVICE`, `DD_ENV`, `DD_VERSION`
`DD_SERVICE`, `DD_TAGS`, `DD_TRACE_AGENT_PORT`
`DD_AGENT_HOST`, `DD_ENV`, `DD_TRACE_ENABLED`
explanation: Unified service tagging uses three reserved tags: `env`, `service`, and `version`. For APM apps you set `DD_ENV`, `DD_SERVICE`, and `DD_VERSION`, and the tracer applies them to traces (and to logs when log injection is on).
notes: Correct: these map to the reserved `service`, `env`, and `version` tags.
`DD_TAGS` adds arbitrary global tags, and `DD_TRACE_AGENT_PORT` is the Agent's trace port. Neither is a UST variable.
`DD_AGENT_HOST` points the tracer at the Agent, and `DD_TRACE_ENABLED` turns tracing on or off.

q: Service A calls service B over HTTP, and both are traced with `ddtrace`. How do B's spans end up in the same trace as A's?
options: The Agent matches spans from A and B by their timestamps and host names
Both services set the same `DD_SERVICE` so their spans merge
A injects trace context into the HTTP headers; B extracts it
explanation: Distributed tracing propagates context in request headers. The client injects it (`HTTPPropagator.inject`), and the server extracts it (`HTTPPropagator.extract`) into its active context. Integrations such as Flask, Django, and Requests do this automatically.
notes: The Agent does not stitch traces by time. The trace ID has to be propagated.
Giving two services the same service name mislabels them and does not link their traces.
Correct: header propagation carries the trace ID across the call. Default styles are `datadog,tracecontext,baggage`.

q:
This code starts a worker thread inside a traced block:
def _target(trace_ctx):
    tracer.context_provider.activate(trace_ctx)
    with tracer.trace("second_thread"):
        do_work()

with tracer.trace("main_thread"):
    t = threading.Thread(target=_target, args=(tracer.current_trace_context(),))
    t.start()
Why does `_target` call `tracer.context_provider.activate(trace_ctx)`?
options: To start a new trace for the thread so the two traces stay separate
So `second_thread` joins the main thread's trace instead of starting a new one
To flush the `main_thread` span to the Agent before the thread runs
explanation: ddtrace's documented way to continue a trace in another thread is to pass `tracer.current_trace_context()` to the thread and activate it there. Spans created in the thread then join the same trace instead of being unlinked.
notes: Activation does the opposite: it links the thread's spans to the existing trace.
Correct: activating the passed context makes new spans in the thread children of the original trace.
Activation sets the active context. It does not send anything to the Agent.

q: What does logs injection (`DD_LOGS_INJECTION=true`) do in a `ddtrace`-instrumented Python app?
options: Adds `dd.trace_id`, `dd.span_id` and similar fields to log records to link logs and traces
Ships the app's log files to Datadog through the Agent's trace receiver on port `8126`
Turns every log line into its own span inside the currently active trace
explanation: Logs injection adds `dd.trace_id`, `dd.span_id`, `dd.service`, `dd.env`, and `dd.version` to log records so you can correlate logs with traces. Recent `ddtrace` versions enable it by default; older versions need `DD_LOGS_INJECTION=true`.
notes: Correct: log records carry trace and span IDs (plus the UST fields) for correlation.
Logs injection only enriches log records. Log shipping is a separate path.
Log lines stay log lines. Only the IDs of the active trace and span are added to them.

q:
A service runs under `ddtrace-run` with logs injection enabled, but its log lines show no trace IDs. Its logging setup is:
logging.basicConfig(format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
What should you change?
options: Set `DD_TRACE_DEBUG=true` so the tracer prints the IDs into every log line
Point `DD_TRACE_AGENT_PORT` at the Datadog log intake so IDs get attached
Add `dd.*` fields such as `%(dd.trace_id)s` to the format string
explanation: Logs injection adds the attributes to each record, but a standard library log format must reference them. Include `dd.service`, `dd.env`, `dd.version`, `dd.trace_id`, and `dd.span_id` in the format string.
notes: `DD_TRACE_DEBUG` turns on the tracer's own debug logs. It does not change your app's log format.
`DD_TRACE_AGENT_PORT` is the Agent's trace port and has nothing to do with log formatting.
Correct: the format string has to include the injected `dd.*` attributes for them to appear.

options: The whole trace is dropped in the tracer and never sent to the Agent
Only the matching span is removed; the rest of the trace is sent
The trace is sent, and Datadog's retention filters discard it
explanation: A `TraceFilter`'s `process_trace` receives the whole trace. Returning `None` drops the entire trace, and returning `trace` passes it on. Filters are registered with `tracer.configure(trace_processors=[...])` and run in order before anything is sent.
notes: Correct: returning `None` discards the full trace before it leaves the application.
The filter works on the whole trace. This code returns `None` for all of it, not only one span.
Filtering happens in the tracer before sending. Retention filters are separate tag-based controls in the Datadog UI.

q:
To troubleshoot missing traces, a pod's tracer starts with:
DD_TRACE_LOG_LEVEL=WARNING
DD_TRACE_DEBUG=true
At which level does the `ddtrace` logger log?
options: `WARNING`, because `DD_TRACE_LOG_LEVEL` is the more specific setting
`DEBUG`, because `DD_TRACE_DEBUG` takes precedence over `DD_TRACE_LOG_LEVEL`
None: conflicting log settings stop the tracer from starting at all
explanation: `DD_TRACE_DEBUG` enables the tracer's debug logging and takes precedence over `DD_TRACE_LOG_LEVEL`. The docs use `DD_TRACE_DEBUG=true ddtrace-run ...` to debug missing traces.
notes: `DD_TRACE_LOG_LEVEL` only applies when debug mode is not turned on.
Correct: debug mode wins. Use `DD_TRACE_LOG_FILE` to send these logs to a file.
The two settings can be combined; one simply overrides the other.
